scenes.title: Mass and gas chemistry are linked
scenes.narration: A galaxy’s mass–metallicity relation links its stellar mass to the abundance of elements in its gas. This review asks why surveys can disagree before the galaxies differ, then separates three observational effects that are often mixed together.
scenes.callout: First separate measurement effects from physics

scenes.title: Name each bias before comparing samples
scenes.narration: Calibration scale means the conversion from emission-line measurements to an abundance. Aperture means how much of a galaxy the instrument samples. Diffuse ionized gas is thinly spread, electrically charged gas. The framework treats these as separate sources of bias.
scenes.callout: Three systematics, not one blended correction

scenes.title: Two abundance scales can differ fivefold
scenes.narration: One family of diagnostics uses models of gas ionized by light; another is anchored to electron temperature. Their absolute oxygen-abundance scales can differ by about zero point seven dex, mathematically a factor of five. Without conversion, that offset can mimic or hide evolution.
scenes.callout: A scale mismatch can look like cosmic change

scenes.title: The same line ratio may not mean the same thing
scenes.narration: Individual line-ratio tools also have limits. The R twenty-three indicator can map one reading to two possible abundances. Nitrogen-based indicators assume a local nitrogen-to-oxygen pattern that may fail at high redshift, so mixing diagnostics can create a false trend.
scenes.callout: Diagnostic choice must stay visible

scenes.title: A central fiber is not a whole galaxy
scenes.narration: A fixed fiber covers different physical areas at different distances. When it samples below roughly twenty percent of the galaxy, central-to-global metallicity errors can exceed zero point one five dex. Small central samples can therefore contribute to an apparent high-mass turnover.
scenes.callout: Coverage changes with galaxy size and distance

scenes.title: Blended emission can reshape a gradient
scenes.narration: Diffuse ionized gas supplies thirty to sixty percent of H alpha, a hydrogen emission line, in the reviewed literature. Its harder ionizing field strengthens low-ionization lines. When spectra blend this gas with other emission, inferred changes in metallicity across a galaxy can flatten or even reverse.
scenes.callout: Integrated light mixes distinct gas environments

scenes.title: Three rules make comparisons auditable
scenes.narration: The recommended workflow has three steps. Put every abundance on one declared scale using published conversions. Require enough galaxy coverage, or apply corrections calibrated with spatial maps. Finally, use integral-field spectroscopy, which resolves positions across a galaxy, as an independent check.
scenes.callout: Keep calibration and aperture terms separate
